title: Margaret of Scotland (16 November)
hook: a queen who fed orphans and the poor before she ate

segments.voice: Yesterday, Albert, the friar with a leaf in his hand. Your line was patron of science. What plant did you get to know? Day one thousand forty-two.

The man who heard her confessions wrote her life after she died, and he kept one morning scene in it. Before the queen of Scotland eats a thing, small children with no parents are brought in. She takes them on her knee, she feeds them herself, sometimes with her own spoon, and only after that does she sit down to her own meal. A queen, with servants for everything, choosing to do this part with her own hands. Today's word is the queen who ate second.
screen: `MORNING IN A ROYAL HOUSE.` → `THE CHILDREN EAT FIRST.` → `THE QUEEN EATS SECOND.`

segments.voice: Margaret was born a princess of the old English royal family, in exile, far from England. The usual account says that after the Norman conquest her family fled, and their ship came to Scotland, where she married King Malcolm. Her confessor, a monk named Turgot, wrote her life, and most of what's told here comes from it. He describes a woman of long prayers and hard fasting who still kept a busy court and raised a large family. And he describes the poor, everywhere around her. She fed orphans before she ate. She served the poor at table herself, sometimes with the king beside her. She gave away so much that, Turgot says, the king's own treasure was raided for alms, and Malcolm pretended not to notice. One small detail has stayed with readers. Malcolm, Turgot says, could not read. But he saw how his wife loved her books, so he would pick them up and kiss them, and he had some of them covered in gold and jewels for her. A king who could not read, honoring what his wife loved. Behind all of this stands a line from Matthew's Gospel, where the King at the end says to those on his right: "For I was hungry, and you gave me to eat." They ask when, and he answers that whatever they did for the least of his brethren, they did for him. Margaret seems to have heard that literally. If Christ was in the hungry child, then the hungry child was fed before the queen. That's the order her life keeps: first the poor.
screen: `A PRINCESS IN EXILE.` · `HER CONFESSOR WROTE HER LIFE.` · `THE KING WHO KISSED HER BOOKS.` · `I WAS HUNGRY, AND YOU GAVE ME TO EAT.` · then, large: `FIRST THE POOR.`

segments.voice: Today's practice: feed someone before yourself. It can be very small. At your next meal, serve someone else first, or set aside a share for someone who needs it, or put food in a donation bin before you buy your own. For now, settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the person, or the place, you'll feed first today. Imagine handing it over, and only then turning to your own plate. If you pray, you can ask Margaret's help to see Christ in the one you feed. If you don't, simply hold that person in mind with care for two minutes. The bell holds the time.
Margaret. A queen, wife of King Malcolm, who fed orphans and served the poor before she ate, as her confessor Turgot remembered her.
Your line: first the poor. Today, before you take your own share of something, food or time or attention, give someone else theirs. Day one thousand forty-two.

howItsDone: Catholics keep the memorial of Saint Margaret of Scotland on 16 November; in Scotland she is honored as a patron, and a small chapel in Edinburgh Castle bears her name.
